project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas Stillingia-first visual family module
project_scope.note: Stillingia texana is the first canonical local anchor. The lesson emphasizes broad Euphorbiaceae characters and explicitly avoids treating Euphorbia's cyathium as a family-wide requirement.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: If latex is present, treat it as a clue rather than proof. Then inspect the flowers: Euphorbiaceae commonly has very reduced unisexual flowers and a superior ovary built from three carpels, often maturing into a 3-part capsule/schizocarp.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Habit ranges from herbs to shrubs and trees. Leaves are often alternate and simple; stipules and latex are common in many lineages but not universal.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are commonly unisexual and may be extremely reduced. The ovary is usually superior and 3-locular/3-carpellate.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Often a 3-part dry schizocarp or capsule separating into one-seeded mericarps.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not define the family by cyathia. Cyathia are the specialized Euphorbia pattern; Stillingia uses a different unisexual inflorescence architecture.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → latex/leaf clue → unisexual flower architecture → ovary/fruit confirmation
visual_lesson.intro: The spurge family makes more sense when you stop expecting a normal flower. Many members reduce the flowers dramatically and let the ovary/fruit architecture do the confirming.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the local Stillingia
steps.look_for: A many-stemmed perennial with narrow alternate leaves growing in thin-soiled limestone habitat.
steps.why_it_matters: Gives the family a real Edwards Plateau anchor instead of a generic tropical example.

steps.title: 2 · Use latex carefully
steps.look_for: White latex if already exposed, plus narrow gland-toothed leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: Latex is a useful family clue but is not universal and should not require damaging a plant.

steps.title: 3 · Read the inflorescence vertically
steps.look_for: Pistillate flowers toward the base of the terminal axis and condensed staminate flower clusters above.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows how Euphorbiaceae can reduce and separate male/female flowers instead of making one showy bisexual flower.

steps.title: 4 · Confirm the three-part fruit plan
steps.look_for: A superior, typically three-locular ovary developing into a dry 3-part capsule/schizocarp.
steps.why_it_matters: The 3-carpellate fruit architecture is a stronger broad-family confirmation than latex alone.

comparisons.title: Euphorbiaceae vs Apocynaceae
comparisons.rule: Both may have milky latex. Euphorbiaceae commonly has highly reduced unisexual flowers and a 3-carpellate capsule; Apocynaceae commonly has a conspicuous fused corolla and a 2-carpel gynoecium, with milkweeds adding corona/gynostegium/pollinia.

comparisons.title: Stillingia vs Euphorbia
comparisons.rule: Both are Euphorbiaceae, but Stillingia does not use Euphorbia's specialized cyathium. Treat the cyathium as a Euphorbia-subset character, not a family definition.

visual_lesson.caveat: Latex, stipules and the 3-part fruit pattern are common rather than absolute across the entire broad family. Use several reproductive characters together.
